#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind regression

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When `RunPodSandbox` is cancelled, times out, or reports a sandbox-name conflict, kubelet now inspects pod sandboxes for the same pod UID and attempt. If a matching sandbox is already ready, kubelet uses it. Any matching non-ready sandboxes are stopped and removed so the runtime can release sandbox-name reservations before the next retry.

The recovery uses a short bounded context detached from the cancelled `RunPodSandbox` call so cleanup can proceed without blocking indefinitely.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #139097

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This handles both the initial cancelled/deadline `RunPodSandbox` error and the retry-side `failed to reserve sandbox name ... is reserved for ...` error reported by containerd.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Kubelet now recovers from cancelled or timed-out CRI RunPodSandbox calls by reusing a matching ready sandbox or stopping and removing matching non-ready sandboxes before retrying pod sandbox creation.
```

Recently added an apiserver restart phase to the 5k scalability test. The default memory configuration of coredns at [170MB]( https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/blob/master/pkg/model/components/kubedns.go#L72-L75) consistently OOMKills coredns when apiserver is restarted due to the relist. coredns cannot handle a relist with the current configurations (services and endpointslice), despite being fine in steady state.

235/313 coredns pods restarted, 233 of them `OOMKilled` (exit 137), per
    [SystemPodMetrics_load.json](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/138758/pull-kubernetes-gce-master-scale-performance-5000/2055661403896811520/artifacts/SystemPodMetrics_load_2026-05-16T17:20:47Z.json).

Failing run: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/138758/pull-kubernetes-gce-master-scale-performance-5000/20556614038

Proposing to increase memory limit on 5k scalability test for coredns. Theory is that relist doubles the memory footprint before calling replace on the store. Steady state coredns hovers around 82MB, and with doubling memory and gc variance, can easily hit the 170MB limit. 

coredns for the test is on [1.13.2](https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/blob/master/upup/models/cloudup/resources/addons/coredns.addons.k8s.io/k8s-1.12.yaml.template#L171) which maps to client go v0.34 with WatchList off by default.

body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When a node transitions from `Ready=False` to `Ready=Unknown` (e.g., containerd crashes making the node `False`, then kubelet also stops and the grace period expires making it `Unknown`), `MarkPodsNotReady` was not called. The `switch` in `monitorNodeHealth` only fired when `observedReadyCondition.Status == ConditionTrue`, missing the `False→Unknown` transition entirely.

This means pods on such nodes remained `Ready` despite the node being unreachable, causing traffic to continue being forwarded to a broken node.

The fix changes the trigger condition from "was previously `True`" to "the status has actually changed to a non-True value" (`observedReady != currentReady`), covering all transitions: `True→False`, `True→Unknown`, and the previously missed `False→Unknown`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #112733

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- The production change is a single condition on line 768 of `node_lifecycle_controller.go` — `observedReadyCondition.Status == v1.ConditionTrue` becomes `observedReadyCondition.Status != currentReadyCondition.Status`.
- PR #137527 covers the same one-line fix; opening a fresh PR since it has had no reviews or `ok-to-test` for ~2 months.
- A new unit test case is added to `TestMonitorNodeHealthMarkPodsNotReady` covering the `False→Unknown` scenario (`expectedPodStatusUpdate: true`).

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fix: node lifecycle controller now calls MarkPodsNotReady when a node transitions from NotReady (false) to Unreachable (unknown), preventing pods from incorrectly remaining Ready when kubelet stops after a prior node failure.
```

body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
ParseQuantity was incorrectly routing 19-digit values (near math.MaxInt64)
into the slow decimal path instead of the fast integer path, causing
AsInt64() to return false for values that are perfectly valid int64 numbers.

Root cause: maxInt64Factors was set to 18, but math.MaxInt64
(9223372036854775807) has 19 digits, causing precision to calculate as -1
and bypass the fast integer path entirely.

Two fixes:
1. Bumped maxInt64Factors from 18 to 19 in math.go
2. Changed quantity.go to fall through to the decimal path on
   strconv.ParseInt overflow error, instead of returning ErrNumeric.
   This ensures values larger than math.MaxInt64 are valid quantities
   stored as decimals rather than hard errors.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #135487

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
Fixed a bug where resource.ParseQuantity failed to use the fast integer
path for 19-digit values near math.MaxInt64, causing AsInt64() to
incorrectly return false for valid int64 values.

title: HPA controller - hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector func serializes all workers behind global exclusive mutex, causing ~ O(#Hpa*#Hpa) degradation at scale

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/scalability

labels.name: triage/accepted

body:
### What happened? ### TL;DR on the Issue The HPA controller's selector overlap check ([`hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L396-L422)) runs every reconciliation for every HPA and holds a [global exclusive mutex](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) while performing O(H) work. Despite starting [multiple worker goroutines](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L217), only one can execute the overlap check at a time. At scale, **_mutex contention_** dominates wall-clock time and reconciliation cannot keep up with the resync period. ### Mutex profile **60-second sample:** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Duration: 60.02s, Total samples = 1.35hrs (8111.81%) 1.35hrs 100% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).computeReplicasForMetrics 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.41%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.92%) ``` 1.35 hours of goroutine-blocked time accumulated in 60 seconds of wall clock (8111% of wall clock duration). **Cumulative snapshot (since process start):** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Total samples = 4.18hrs 4.18hrs 99.90% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.25%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.80%) ``` 99.25% of all mutex contention in the HPA controller is in `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. ### Root cause Three problems compound: #### 1. Global exclusive lock on a per-HPA operation The [`hpaSelectorsMux`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L125) is held for the [entire body](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) of `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. This includes iterating all pods, inserting each into the BiMultimap, querying associations, and cleaning up. All worker goroutines contend on this single lock regardless of namespace. #### 2. BiMultimap cache is always cold [`KeepOnly([]Key{})`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L415) destroys all temporary pod entries at the end of every call. This triggers [refCount decrement to zero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L188-L191), which deletes the `selectingByLabeled` cache entry. Every subsequent call hits the ["Cache miss. Scan selecting objects"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L138) path, iterating all HPA selectors in the BiMultimap. #### 3. A read operation implemented as write-query-delete The overlap check only needs to answer: "which existing HPA selectors match these pod labels?" That's a read query. But because the BiMultimap API currently supports "insert a labeled object, then ask who selects it," the code must [temporarily insert pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L403-L404) (a write), [query](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L406), then [delete](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L415). The writes require an exclusive lock, making concurrent execution impossible. Additionally, the BiMultimap is global across all namespaces, so [`Put` scans all selectors](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L143-L149) and [skips non-matching namespaces](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L144) , wasted iteration. #### Secondary effect: unbounded memory growth -> OOM The informer [resyncs all HPA objects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L172) every 15s, delivering H update events to [`enqueueHPA`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L174) via the informer's [`processorListener.run()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1330). When `enqueueHPA` [blocks on `hpaSelectorsMux`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L275), the listener stalls. The [`pop()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1296) goroutine continues buffering incoming events into [`pendingNotifications`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1223-L1225) , an unbounded ring buffer that [doubles when full](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/vendor/k8s.io/utils/buffer/ring_growing.go#L81-L83) and never shrinks. Each resync cycle delivers H more events; if the handler can't drain faster than events arrive, memory grows without bound. Heap profile diffs (~12 hours apart) confirm constant growth: ``` 2444.07MB k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache.(*sharedIndexInformer).OnUpdate 2016MB k8s.io/utils/buffer.(*TypedRingGrowing[...]).WriteOne ``` ### Time Complexity analysis Per single reconciliation, `bimap.Put()` hits a cache miss and [scans all `selectingObjects`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L138-L149) , O(H) iteration (the BiMultimap is global across namespaces). A full reconciliation cycle of all H HPAs, serialized by the exclusive lock, performs: ``` H reconciliations × O(H) per reconciliation = O(H*H) total ``` Doubling HPAs quadruples wall-clock time. ### What did you expect to happen? Workers should execute overlap checks concurrently as much as possible. The overlap check is fundamentally a read query ("which HPA selectors match these pod labels?") and should not require exclusive locking. #### Proposed solution Replace the BiMultimap + external mutex with a per-namespace selector map using `sync.RWMutex`: ```go type hpaSelectorStore struct { mu sync.RWMutex namespaces map[string]map[selectors.Key]labels.Selector } func (s *hpaSelectorStore) HPAsMatchingPods(namespace string, pods []*v1.Pod) []selectors.Key { s.mu.RLock() defer s.mu.RUnlock() uniqueLabels := make(map[string]labels.Set) for _, pod := range pods { key := labels.Set(pod.Labels).String() if _, seen := uniqueLabels[key]; !seen { uniqueLabels[key] = labels.Set(pod.Labels) } } hpas := make(map[selectors.Key]struct{}) for _, set := range uniqueLabels { for key, sel := range s.namespaces[namespace] { if sel.Matches(set) { hpas[key] = struct{}{} } } } return keys(hpas) } ``` ^^^ - `HPAsMatchingPods` uses `RLock`, all workers proceed concurrently. No temporary pod insertion, no cleanup, no cache to destroy. - only iterates selectors in the relevant namespace (HPA's in namespace), not all H. No cross-namespace scanning. - same effective optimization as BiMultimap's label cache (identical labels matched once), without write-then-destroy overhead. - HPA registration and selector updates acquire exclusive lock for a single map write, only on HPA create/update events, not per reconciliation. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Run the HPA controller at scale (10K+ HPAs) and collect a mutex profile: ```bash curl -s "http://localhost:10257/debug/pprof/mutex?debug=1" > mutex.pb.gz go tool pprof -text mutex.pb.gz ``` Contention in `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector` will dominate as HPA count increases. ### Anything else we need to know? I did benchmarking with above solution and found significant improvement. Below are the results. #### Benchmark results 10,000 HPAs, 100 pods/HPA, 10 namespaces, 96-core machine. **Throughput (reconciliations/second):** | Workers | Current (BiMultimap) | Proposed (SelectorStore) | Speedup | |---------|---------------------|------------------------|---------| | 50 | 2,635 | 444,671 | 169× | | 100 | 2,600 | 506,873 | 195× | Current throughput **degrades** with more workers (increased contention). Proposed throughput **scales** with workers until CPU saturation. **Contention (100 workers):** | | Avg lock wait per operation | |---|---| | Current | 38.2 ms | | Proposed | 0.178 ms | | Reduction | **214×** | **Memory:** | | Bytes/HPA (10 namespaces) | Bytes/HPA (100 namespaces) | |---|---|---| | Current | 474 | 474 | | Proposed | 226 | 131 | **Allocations per operation (100 workers):** | | Bytes/op | Allocs/op | |---|---|---| | Current | 6,148,911 | 71,303 | | Proposed | 563,203 | 30,100 | #### Impact With 100 workers and 15s resync period: - **Current**: 2,600 ops/s → workers spend 99.7% of time blocked on the mutex. Selector overlap check alone consumes seconds of wall clock per cycle. - **Proposed**: 500K+ ops/s → selector check becomes negligible. ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version sh-5.2$ kubectl version Client Version: v1.34.0-beta.0-eks-7ffece0 Kustomize Version: v5.6.0 Server Version: v1.34.7-eks-40737a8 ```

This fixes in-cluster configuration lookup on Windows when a process is running from a working directory on a drive other than `C:`.

body:
## Problem

`batchStateCompatible` calls `RunFilterPlugins` on `lastChosenNode` to determine whether the node is "full" for the incoming pod. For pods with low resource requirements this check always returns success (not-rejected), causing the batch cache to be flushed every scheduling cycle with no benefit.

The synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call:
1. Traverses the entire filter plugin chain on the critical scheduling path
2. Always yields a no-op result for small pods on nodes with remaining capacity
3. Forces a duplicate filter of `lastChosenNode` (it is also evaluated in the parallel `findNodesThatPassFilters` pipeline)

This is the common pattern in microservice clusters where the majority of pods have modest resource requests.

Fixes #137707

## Solution

Add an O(1) pre-check before `RunFilterPlugins` in `batchStateCompatible`:

If the pod requests any CPU or memory **and** the node's remaining allocatable capacity (allocatable − requested) covers both, the node cannot be resource-full for this pod. Return `false` immediately without calling `RunFilterPlugins`.

The pre-check applies only when the pod has nonzero CPU or memory requests. Zero-request pods fall through to `RunFilterPlugins` unchanged. Non-resource constraints (taints, affinity, etc.) are conservatively ignored: at worst a valid batch hint is missed, but scheduling correctness is unaffected — returning `false` from `batchStateCompatible` only prevents hint reuse.

## Benchmarks

Apple M3 Max, go1.26.3:

```
BenchmarkPodContainerRequests (pre-check alone):
  25 ns/op,   0 B/op, 0 allocs/op

BenchmarkRunFilterPluginsOnly (1-plugin framework call):
  198 ns/op, 200 B/op, 6 allocs/op
```

With 10+ filter plugins in production (NodeResourcesFit, NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, VolumeBinding, etc.) the savings are proportionally larger. For workloads of small pods — the dominant pattern in microservice deployments — this eliminates `RunFilterPlugins` from the critical scheduling path entirely.

## Tests

`TestBatchResourcePrecheck` (4 cases) verifies:
- Pod fits (100m CPU, 128Mi memory on a node with 4 CPUs remaining): filter plugin **not called** (`filter.calls == 0`)
- Pod exhausts node CPU (5000m on node with 4000m remaining): filter plugin called, batch state compatible → hint given
- Pod exhausts node memory (9Gi on node with 8Gi remaining): filter plugin called, batch state compatible → hint given
- Pod with no resource requests: filter plugin called (pre-check bypassed), existing behavior preserved

All existing `TestBatchBasic` cases continue to pass.

#### What this PR does / why we need it: 
kubectl top pod currently sends field selectors directly to the Metrics API. However, the Metrics API only supports metadata based field selectors, makes causing selectors such as `spec.nodeName` to fail.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Retry admission webhook calls on selected transport-level errors, such as connection reset, probable EOF, and HTTP/2 connection lost.

A terminating webhook pod can close an existing keep-alive connection. Without retry, the API server fails the admission POST immediately even though another webhook endpoint may be available.

This change keeps the retry behavior local to admission webhook dispatchers instead of changing generic client-go retry behavior for all POST requests. Each attempt rebuilds the webhook POST request so the timeout query parameter is recalculated from the remaining context deadline.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #127335

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Retries are scoped to selected transport-level failures only. Admission rejection, invalid AdmissionReview responses, HTTP 5xx, 429, and other StatusError responses from the webhook continue to be handled by the existing admission logic.

A webhook backend may receive the same AdmissionReview more than once if it processed the request but the connection failed before the apiserver received a complete response. The apiserver only applies the result after receiving and verifying a complete AdmissionReview response, and mutating webhooks are expected to be idempotent and side-effect constrained.

Validation:

```

```

```release-note
The API server now retries admission webhook calls on selected transport-level errors, such as connection reset, probable EOF, and HTTP/2 connection lost.
```

title: kubelet/CRI: cancelled RunPodSandbox leaks containerd sandbox-name reservation, pod stuck

body:
### What happened?

On Kubernetes `v1.36.0`, kubelet's CRI `RunPodSandbox` call to containerd hits its 4-minute client-side deadline (`RuntimeRequestTimeout * 2`, see `staging/src/k8s.io/cri-client/pkg/remote_runtime.go:223`) before containerd finishes provisioning the sandbox. When this happens, kubelet's gRPC client cancels the stream with `RST_STREAM CANCEL`, but the sandbox-name reservation on containerd is never released. kubelet immediately retries with the same pod UID, and containerd refuses with:

```
rpc error: code = FailedPrecondition desc = failed to reserve sandbox name
  "<podname>_<namespace>_<uid>_0":
  name "<podname>_<namespace>_<uid>_0" is reserved for "<container-sha>"
```

The pod stays permanently in `ContainerCreating`. The cluster cannot recover without manual intervention.

The same workload on `v1.35.4` with byte-identical containerd `v2.2.3-k3s1`, runc `v1.4.2`, and a closely-matched GHA `ubuntu-24.04` runner kernel (6.17.x line) does not exhibit this signature. The only changed variable of substance is Kubernetes itself.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either:
1. kubelet should issue `RemovePodSandbox` (or equivalent cleanup) on containerd after its own `RunPodSandbox` context is cancelled, so the sandbox-name reservation is released and subsequent retries can succeed; or
2. The `RuntimeRequestTimeout * 2` (4-min) deadline should not fire under normal pod startup load on a resource-constrained node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We do not have an on-demand reproducer; the bug is intermittent. Documented conditions when it manifests:

- GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest` runner (x86_64, 2 vCPU, ~7 GiB RAM)
- k3s `v1.36.0-k3s1` started in Docker via Testcontainers, single-node, default args
- Workload: StatefulSet with `volumeClaimTemplates`, brought up while kube-system pods (`coredns`, `local-path-provisioner`) are still settling
- The **first affected pod is consistently `local-path-provisioner`** (a system pod), so this is not workload-dependent
- Failure first manifests at **~4:25 after `containerd is now running`**, almost exactly on the `RuntimeRequestTimeout * 2` boundary

Sequence in our k3s log:
1. `rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = stream terminated by RST_STREAM with error code: CANCEL` (client-initiated gRPC cancellation by kubelet)
2. ~14 s later, on retry: `failed to reserve sandbox name ... is reserved for <sha>`
3. ~530 retries in 18 minutes (~one every 2 s), all rejected the same way

Independent symptom on the same CRI channel: `StopContainer` on the `metrics-server` container hangs with `DeadlineExceeded`, three of the eight retries carrying the same `RST_STREAM CANCEL` token. Both `RunPodSandbox` and `StopContainer` are being cut by kubelet mid-flight.

What we tried locally (does not reproduce on Apple Silicon Docker Desktop):

```bash
docker run -d --privileged --cpus 2 --memory 4g \
  --name k3s-repro rancher/k3s:v1.36.0-k3s1 \
  server --disable=traefik --disable=metrics-server
sleep 45
# burst 8 StatefulSets x 3 replicas with PVCs
for i in $(seq 1 8); do
  docker exec -i k3s-repro kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: load-$i }
spec:
  serviceName: load-$i
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: load-$i } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: load-$i } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh","-c","sleep 36000"]
        resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi } }
        volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /data }]
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata: { name: data }
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      resources: { requests: { storage: 100Mi } }
EOF
done
sleep 60
docker logs k3s-repro 2>&1 | grep -E "is reserved for|FailedPrecondition"
```

Produces a healthy cluster, no sandbox-reservation errors. Trigger appears to be architecture-specific (x86_64), kernel-specific (GHA Ubuntu vs Docker Desktop LinuxKit), or related to genuine vs nominal CPU contention.

### Anything else we need to know?

**Triage pointer from k3s** ([k3s-io/k3s#14078](https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/14078)):
> None of the code in the failing code path lives in this repo, and it is unlikely that we can direct change anything to resolve it. I kind of suspect that it is related to grpc module version bump in k8s 1.36.

`kubernetes/kubernetes` `go.mod` diff `v1.35.4` to `v1.36.0`, gRPC-related:

|---|---|---|
| `google.golang.org/grpc` | **v1.72.2** | **v1.79.3** |
| `golang.org/x/net` | v0.47.0 | v0.49.0 |
| `golang.org/x/sys` | v0.38.0 | v0.40.0 |
| `go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/google.golang.org/grpc/otelgrpc` | v0.60.0 | v0.65.0 |
| `github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway/v2` | v2.26.3 | v2.27.7 |
| `github.com/grpc-ecosystem/go-grpc-middleware/v2` | v2.3.0 | v2.3.3 |

Notable client/transport behavior changes in gRPC Go in the v1.72.2 .. v1.79.3 window:

- **v1.77.0 [grpc/grpc-go#8534](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/8534)**: `client: Set a read deadline when closing a transport to prevent it from blocking indefinitely on a broken connection.` **Most-suspect change.** Governs cleanup timing on transport close.
- v1.77.0 [#8624](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/8624), [#8657](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/8657), [#8667](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/8667): transport-layer Data-frame I/O refactoring.

- v1.79.0 [#8769](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/8769): HTTP/2 server-side stream early-termination header check.
- v1.73.0 [#8312](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/8312): `client: fail RPCs on the client when using extremely short contexts that expire before the grpc-timeout header is created.`

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Add a new alpha feature gate HostAliasesAllowFQDN that allows a trailing dot in hostnames under spec.hostAliases[].hostnames. The trailing dot denotes a Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) as defined in RFC 1034, preventing DNS resolvers from appending the search path.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Trigger scenario
    A node previously ran a version that wrote a V3 CPU manager checkpoint to disk.  That checkpoint’s checksum was computed using the legacy type identity CPUManagerCheckpoint.  The node is then upgraded to the current code, which first tries to read the file as V4, fails, and falls back to V3.   During V3 restore, checksum verification is performed against the new concrete type name CPUManagerCheckpointV3.

this leads to:
  - Kubelet fails to restore CPU manager state during startup.
  - The V3 checkpoint is incorrectly reported as corrupted.
  - Restore then falls through V2 and V1 parsing paths, which also fail.
  - Startup ends with a fatal restore error, and kubelet does not come up unless the checkpoint is removed manually.

      - MarshalCheckpoint() already rewrites CPUManagerCheckpointV3 to CPUManagerCheckpoint before hashing, to preserve compatibility.
      - VerifyChecksum() used only ck.Verify(cp), which hashes the real current type name CPUManagerCheckpointV3.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This WIP PR pushes streamed handling for JSON typed LIST objects one layer earlier, from the JSON encoder into the versioning codec.

The implementation keeps the existing streamed JSON assembly, but changes how version conversion is performed for typed list objects:


The key architectural split is:

- **versioning layer**
  - decides whether the streamed typed-LIST path can be used
  - converts the list header once
  - walks internal list items
  - converts each item individually with `ConvertToVersion(item, targetGV)`
  - passes each converted item to the serializer through an iterator/callback

- **JSON serializer layer**
  - owns JSON formatting
  - writes the list envelope (`kind`, `apiVersion`, `metadata`, `items`)
  - consumes converted items through the iterator
  - writes each item into the JSON `items` array in order

In other words, the serializer still controls JSON assembly, while the versioning codec controls how versioned items are produced.

Previous model:

```text
internal typed list
  -> ConvertToVersion(full list)
  -> external typed list with full Items []T materialized
  -> streamed JSON encoding
```

New model:

```text
internal typed list
  -> ConvertToVersion(empty list header)
  -> for each internal item:
       ConvertToVersion(item)
       pass item to JSON serializer callback
  -> streamed JSON encoding
```

Callback flow:

```text
versioning codec
  -> EncodeListWithIterator(versionedListHeader, writer, iter)

JSON serializer
  -> writes list envelope
  -> starts "items":[
  -> calls iter(visit)

iter (implemented by versioning)
  -> walks internal list items
  -> converts each item to target version
  -> calls visit(versionedItem)

visit (implemented by serializer)
  -> writes comma if needed
  -> encodes one item into the JSON array
```

This callback model is used to preserve layering.

There are two callbacks involved:

- `iter(...)` is the callback provided by the versioning codec
  - it describes how versioned items are produced from the internal list
- `visit(...)` is the callback provided by the serializer
  - it describes what should happen once one versioned item is ready to be written
  - in practice, this is the callback that performs the per-item JSON encode/write step



- **versioning does not need to know JSON formatting details**
  - versioning passes its `iter(...)` callback into `EncodeListWithIterator(...)`
  - inside `iter(...)`, versioning only:
    - walks the internal list
    - converts each item with `ConvertToVersion(item, targetGV)`
    - calls `visit(versionedItem)`
  - here, `visit(...)` is the serializer-provided callback, i.e. the callback that performs the actual per-item encode/write step
  - concretely, this happens here:
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c27335aa44b8d0af1d578a133b7ca40e5ac73da3/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/versioning/versioning.go#L320-L331

- **the serializer does not need to know how list traversal or version conversion works**
  - the serializer only knows that it has an `iter(...)` callback that can supply items while it is writing the JSON `items` array
  - here, `iter(...)` is the callback returned from the previous step by the versioning codec
  - the serializer writes `"items":[`, calls `iter(...)`, and for each callback invocation:
    - writes a comma if needed
    - encodes the item into JSON
  - concretely, the serializer consumes `iter(...)` here:
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c27335aa44b8d0af1d578a133b7ca40e5ac73da3/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/json/collections.go#L151-L159
  - and the surrounding JSON list assembly is here:
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c27335aa44b8d0af1d578a133b7ca40e5ac73da3/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/json/collections.go#L109-L165

- **no intermediate full external typed list needs to be materialized**
  - the list header is converted once, separately from items

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Trigger scenario
  The bug is triggered when PodLevelResourceManagers is enabled and kubelet restores the memory manager checkpoint from a file that:
  - looks like a V2 checkpoint and can be unmarshaled into MemoryManagerCheckpointV2
  - contains invalid V2 checksum, so V2 restore fails
  - is still readable as V1, so the code falls back to V1 and migrates V1 data into V2

  A practical case is a partially corrupted or hand-edited V2 checkpoint file that still carries podEntries data.

  After fallback, kubelet restores a hybrid checkpoint:
  - PolicyName, MachineState, and Entries come from V1
  - stale PodEntries remain from the failed V2 load attempt

  As a result, sc.cache.SetPodMemoryAssignments(cp.PodEntries) receives corrupted leftover pod-level assignments that should not exist after V1 fallback.


  Root cause
  checkpointmanager.GetCheckpoint() first calls UnmarshalCheckpoint() and only then VerifyChecksum().
  That means a corrupt V2 file can already populate checkpointV2 before checksum verification fails.

  In loadAndMigrateCheckpointV2(), the old logic reused that same checkpointV2 object during V1 -> V2 migration.
  But migrateV1CheckpointToV2Checkpoint() only overwrites:
  - PolicyName
  - MachineState
  - Entries

  It does not clear or replace PodEntries, so stale V2 data survives the fallback path.

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When `CSIDriver.spec.requiresRepublish=true`, kubelet periodically calls
`NodePublishVolume` to refresh volume contents. If a republish call
returns a final error, kubelet deletes the host mount directory and
`vol_data.json` in `csi_mounter.SetUpAt`. The pod's bind mount is
already pointing at that directory, so the pod ends up seeing stale or
empty contents and subsequent successful republishes cannot repair it.

The reconciler already knows whether a call is a remount via its
`isRemount` parameter. This PR threads that into `volume.MounterArgs`
and uses it in the CSI mounter to skip the cleanup on remount. The
existing `!mounterArgs.ReconstructedVolume` guard is preserved.

### What happened?

The server exposes `apiserver_watch_list_duration_seconds` which measures how long it takes to stream the initial set of events for a WatchList request. 

There is no corresponding client-side metric. Without a client-side metric, we cannot measure WatchList latency experienced by controllers.

We could add a client-side watchlist latency metric. It seems we at least have two options for where to measure it:

Option 1: We could measure from the REST client layer. This would involve capturing watch events and detecting the `k8s.io/initial-events-end` bookmark annotation that marks the end of the initial event stream. 

Option 2: We could measure from reflector layer. The reflector is currently the only consumer of WatchList and already detects the initial-events-end bookmark. Adding a metric at this level would be easier.

body:
### What happened?

Server-side metrics (e.g. `apiserver_request_duration_seconds`) let you measure latency per verb, resource, group, version, and scope.

However, the client-side metrics exposed by client-go's REST layer use only verb (raw HTTP method) and host as labels. This means:

  - You cannot measure client-side latency per resource. "How long do Pod LIST calls take from the controller's perspective?" is unanswerable.
  - LIST and GET are indistinguishable. The client records the raw HTTP method GET for both. The server distinguishes these as separate verbs.
  - No scope information. You cannot distinguish cluster-scoped from namespace-scoped requests.

Debugging client-side latency is difficult because the metrics lack this information.

We could add resource-aware labels to `rest_client` metrics, similar to what server-side metrics already provide:

1. We could add resource , group, version, and scope labels.
2. We could map HTTP methods to API verbs (GET vs LIST) so verb carries semantic meaning.


Additionally, the recently introduced `A Unified Identity for client-go Components for Enhanced Telemetry` ([xref](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HUNewBqN3lk2DSHJaxKZmmhYgt0SNgp9AqpJTY6cfRM/edit?resourcekey=0-uIvQ3ezUROHa6OKjWZUzcw&tab=t.0#heading=h.qtaj715knfkg))  for client-go components provides a name label that Informers and Reflectors propagate to identify which component initiated a request. This identity could also be passed into rest_client metrics, allowing to correlate API requests back to the specific component that made them.

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
When DRAConsumableCapacity is enabled, multi-allocatable device allocations are tracked via AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs and AggregatedCapacity instead of AllocatedDevices. The incubating and experimental allocators only checked AllocatedDevices when rebuilding available SharedCounters, so committed shared allocations could be missed across scheduling cycles.

Add an internal IsDeviceAllocated helper that checks all committed allocation-state sources and use it when reconstructing consumed counters. Add a regression test for a fresh allocator seeing committed shared-device counter consumption.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #139034
KEPs: [4815](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4815), [5075](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5075)

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
- The behavior change is intentionally limited to the counter-reconstruction path in the incubating and experimental allocators. Stable has similar-looking code, but does not support `DRAConsumableCapacity`, so this specific feature composition is not reachable there.
 - `internal.IsDeviceAllocated` mirrors the existing exported `structured.IsDeviceAllocated` logic so sub-allocators can reuse it without importing the parent `structured` package and creating an import cycle.
 - The regression test is intentionally cross-cycle: it constructs a fresh allocator with committed shared allocation state in `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs` and `AggregatedCapacity`. With the old `AllocatedDevices.Has(deviceID)` predicate, the test incorrectly allocates the second counter-consuming shared device; with this fix, it rejects it

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixed a Dynamic Resource Allocation scheduler bug that could assign mutually exclusive
device partitions to multiple Pods. This affected DRA drivers using `SharedCounters`
(`DRAPartitionableDevices`) together with multi-allocatable devices (`DRAConsumableCapacity`).
Depending on the device and driver, the incorrect double-allocation could cause workload failures,
device conflicts, crashes, or data loss.
 ```

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Declarative validation is implemented on versioned types. Storage tests have historically been written against the internal type and the vast majority of the tests are version independent.

In-tree API strategies automatically run declarative validation on every create/update. If we were to set `DeclarativeEnforcement: true`, declarative validation errors are raised and "could not find requestInfo in context" is raised because the declarative validation code path needs the API `GroupVersion` from `RequestInfo` to convert the internal object to the versioned type before calling scheme.Validate.

In production this never happens because `RequestInfo` is always set before the strategy is invoked.

This was the only blocker I found preventing `DeclarativeEnforcement: true` from being set on all in-tree APIs.

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Issue description: While syncPod is executing the patch to the API server, new SetContainerReadiness calls arrive and update m.podStatuses to a newer version. Each of those calls tries to signal podStatusChannel, but the channel is capacity-1 and already holds a token from a concurrent update. The signals are silently dropped till next reconcile. 
When syncPod returns, the API server has version N, but m.podStatuses has already moved to version N+K, and nobody has signalled the channel for those K updates. It caused the latency during update pod status to latest.     

Fix: After each syncPod completes, check whether m.podStatuses has moved ahead of what was just synced. If so, send a signal to podStatusChannel to wake up the sync goroutine immediately for another syncBatch, rather than waiting for the next reconciliation.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When pods are blocked in the scheduler's gated queue, the existing STABLE `scheduler_pending_pods{queue="gated"}` gauge tells operators how many pods are stuck but not which gate is responsible. Listing pods to discover which `spec.SchedulingGates` are held by which controller is awkward when multiple gates coexist on the same cluster (cluster autoscaler / Karpenter integrations, custom admission flows, deployment-snapshot gates, spot-placement policies, etc.).

This PR adds a new ALPHA gauge:

```
# HELP scheduler_gated_pods [ALPHA] Number of pods in the gated queue broken down by scheduling gate name from spec.schedulingGates. A pod declaring multiple scheduling gates is counted once per gate, so the sum across gates is greater than or equal to scheduler_pending_pods{queue="gated"}. Pods gated by plugins that do not correspond to a spec.schedulingGates entry are not included.
# TYPE scheduler_gated_pods gauge
scheduler_gated_pods{gate="example.com/foo"} 3
scheduler_gated_pods{gate="example.com/bar"} 1
```

Properties:

- Cardinality is bounded by the (typically small) number of distinct gate names in use on a cluster.
- A pod declaring multiple gates is counted once per gate, so `sum(scheduler_gated_pods)` is greater than or equal to `scheduler_pending_pods{queue="gated"}`.
- Pods that the scheduler gates via a plugin without a matching `spec.schedulingGates` entry continue to contribute to `scheduler_pending_pods{queue="gated"}` but do not appear in the new metric. This is documented in the metric help text.

Per-gate accounting is wired through `unschedulablePods`, which now remembers the gate set it incremented for each pod so it can decrement correctly when the gate set shrinks (gates can only be removed, not added), when the pod transitions out of the gated state, when the pod is deleted, or when the queue is cleared. Unit tests cover each of those transitions.

Existing `scheduler_pending_pods` is unchanged.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #139035

The new metric is registered unconditionally (no feature gate) because it is ALPHA and has bounded cardinality, matching the convention used by sibling ALPHA scheduler metrics. Happy to put it behind a feature gate if sig-scheduling / sig-instrumentation prefer.


body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `scheduler_pending_pods` metric reports counts of pods in each scheduling queue, including `queue="gated"` for pods blocked by `spec.schedulingGates`. Today this aggregate is opaque: there is no way from the metric alone to tell *which* gates are holding pods back.

I'd like the scheduler to expose gate names alongside this counter, either by:

1. Adding a `gate` label to `scheduler_pending_pods` for the `queue="gated"` series and emitting one series per (gate, queue) pair, or
2. Introducing a new metric, e.g. `scheduler_gated_pods{gate="example.com/foo"}`, that reports per-gate counts.

### Why is this needed?

When `scheduler_pending_pods{queue="gated"}` ticks up, operators currently fall back to listing pods (`kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.schedulingGates)'`) or scraping pod state from another source to figure out which controllers or admission webhooks are holding pods. With gate names in the metric, dashboards and alerts can attribute the count directly to the responsible component, and detection of "stuck" gates becomes trivial.

This is especially valuable as more controllers adopt scheduling gates (cluster autoscaler / Karpenter integrations, custom admission flows, deployment snapshot gates, spot-placement policies, etc.). Multiple gates often coexist on the same cluster and the aggregate counter cannot distinguish them.

### Notes

Cardinality:
- Gate names are namespaced (`example.com/foo`), so cardinality is bounded by the number of distinct gates in use on a cluster, typically a handful.
- A pod may declare multiple gates; the metric should either pick a deterministic representative (e.g. the first remaining gate) or emit a series per gate. Whichever trade-off is chosen should be documented.

body:
### What happened?

 When `DRAPartitionableDevices` and `DRAConsumableCapacity` are both enabled, a device with both:
 - `allowMultipleAllocations: true`
 - non-empty `consumesCounters`
 can have its committed counter consumption ignored in later scheduling cycles.

Committed multi-allocatable allocations are stored as shared/capacity allocations in `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs` and `AggregatedCapacity`, not as dedicated entries in `AllocatedDevices`. However, the incubating and experimental structured allocators rebuilt available `SharedCounters` by checking only `AllocatedDevices`.
 
That means a fresh allocator in a later scheduling cycle could treat counters consumed by a committed shared allocation as still available. This can allow overlapping partition devices that share a mutual-exclusion counter to be allocated simultaneously.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the allocator rebuilds available counters from committed allocation state, it should treat a device as allocated if it appears in any committed allocation-state source:
 
 - `AllocatedDevices`
 - `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`
 - `AggregatedCapacity`
 
A committed shared multi-allocatable allocation should continue to subtract its `ConsumesCounters` in later scheduling cycles.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable:
DynamicResourceAllocation=true
DRAPartitionableDevices=true
DRAConsumableCapacity=true

Create two ResourceSlice objects:
```
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
 kind: ResourceSlice
 metadata:
   name: example-counters
 spec:
   driver: example.com
   pool:
     name: node1
     generation: 1
     resourceSliceCount: 2
   nodeName: node1
   sharedCounters:
   - name: nic
     counters:
       slot:
         value: 1
 ---
 apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
 kind: ResourceSlice
 metadata:
   name: example-devices
 spec:
   driver: example.com
   pool:
     name: node1
     generation: 1
     resourceSliceCount: 2
   nodeName: node1
   devices:
   - name: nic-mode-a
     allowMultipleAllocations: true
     capacity:
       slots:
         value: 4
     consumesCounters:
     - counterSet: nic
       counters:
         slot:
           value: 1
   - name: nic-mode-b
     allowMultipleAllocations: true
     capacity:
       slots:
         value: 8
     consumesCounters:
     - counterSet: nic
       counters:
         slot:
           value: 1
```

Then:
1. Schedule a pod with a claim that selects nic-mode-a and consumes capacity from it.
2. Wait for that allocation to be committed.
3. Schedule another pod with a claim that selects nic-mode-b.

Expected: the second allocation is rejected because nic.slot is already consumed.

Actual before the fix: the second allocation can succeed because the fresh allocator does not subtract the counter consumed by the committed shared allocation.

### Anything else we need to know?

This affects the incubating and experimental structured allocators. The stable allocator has similar counter-reconstruction shape but does not currently support DRAConsumableCapacity, so this specific composition is not reachable there.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Overlayfs does not support cgroupv2 writeback accounting. Buffered writes (even with `conv=fsync`) get attributed to the root cgroup instead of the container's cgroup. Switches to `oflag=direct` for writes and adds `iflag=direct` reads to bypass the page cache entirely. Direct I/O is always attributed to the issuing process's cgroup regardless of filesystem type.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR makes two improvements to error handling in the HPA controller:

**1. Fix format-string argument order in object metric error messages**

The error format strings in `GetObjectMetricReplicas` and `GetObjectPerPodMetricReplicas` in the HPA replica calculator had the `fmt.Errorf` arguments in the wrong order relative to the format verbs.

The format string was:
```
"unable to get metric %s: %v on %s %s/%s", metricName, objectRef.Kind, namespace, objectRef.Name, err
```

This caused `objectRef.Kind` to be printed where the error (`%v`) should appear, and `err` to be formatted by the final `%s` meant for `objectRef.Name`. The resulting error messages were misleading and made debugging object metric failures harder.

Fixed by reordering the format string to the idiomatic Go pattern (context first, error last):
```
"unable to get metric %s on %s %s/%s: %w", metricName, objectRef.Kind, namespace, objectRef.Name, err
```

**2. Use `%w` for proper error wrapping across the package**

Replaced `%v` with `%w` for error arguments in all `fmt.Errorf` calls throughout the HPA controller (`horizontal.go`), replica calculator (`replica_calculator.go`), and metrics client (`metrics/client.go`). This enables proper error wrapping so that callers can use `errors.Is` and `errors.As` to inspect underlying errors.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

N/A

- The first commit fixes the argument ordering bug in `GetObjectMetricReplicas` and `GetObjectPerPodMetricReplicas`.
- The second commit is a broader cleanup that replaces `%v` → `%w` for all error arguments in `fmt.Errorf` across the `pkg/controller/podautoscaler` package (30 occurrences across 3 files).
- Two `%v` usages were intentionally left unchanged: integer format arguments in `computeReplicasForMetrics`, and the sentinel error pattern on line 836 of `horizontal.go` where `%v` is used for `err` alongside a deliberate `%w` for `errSpec`.

```release-note
Fixed incorrect error message formatting in the HPA controller when object metric retrieval fails. Also improved error wrapping across the HPA controller to use %w instead of %v, enabling proper error chain inspection.
```
